rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The man gave a little to the companion who admonished him, then stopped giving.
rows.anchor: يعني أعطى صاحبه الذي عاتبه

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ glosses akdā as withholding some of the gift and cutting it off.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء: أمسك من العطية وقطع

rows.speaker: عمرو عن أبيه
rows.claim: The report gives akdā the senses prevented, cut off, ceased, or reached hard rock while digging.
rows.anchor: روى عمرو عن أبيه: أكدى منع وأكدى قطع

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿīd b. Jubayr traces the word to diggers reaching rock after excavating a hollow.
rows.anchor: وذكر سعيد بن جبير الأصل فيه فقال: ألا ترى

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq derives akdā from a digger reaching unworkable stone and stopping the digging.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق: معنى (أكدى) قطع، وأصله من الحفر

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad says akdā means to withhold forcefully and gives a similar digging derivation.
rows.anchor: وقال المبرد: (أكدى) أي منع منعا شديدا

rows.speaker: ابن قتيبة
rows.claim: Ibn Qutayba derives the idiom from hard well-stone and says it describes failing to finish a pursuit or gift; here the man withheld the full amount promised.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن قتيبة: أكدى من كدية الركية وهي الصلابة فيها

rows.speaker: عطاء ومقاتل
rows.claim: ʿAṭāʾ and Muqātil say al-Walīd b. al-Mughīra praised the Qurʾān, then stopped: he gave a little good with his tongue and withheld the rest; the verse rebukes him.
rows.anchor: وقال عطاء ومقاتل إن الوليد بن المغيرة كان قد مدح القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unseen in question is the punishment, and the man supposes his companion will bear it for him.
rows.anchor: يعني ما غاب عنه من أمر العذاب

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj takes seeing as knowing; one can say of a blind person, “I saw Zayd as intelligent,” and the man would claim knowledge that another bears his punishment.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج: (فهو يرى) معناه فهو يعلم، والرؤية تكون بمعنى العلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening asks whether he has not been told or informed; the pages of Moses are the books of the Torah.
rows.anchor: لم يحدث ولم يخبر {بما في صحف موسى} يعني: أسفار التوراة

words: وَأَن لَّيْسَ لِلْإِنسَٰنِ إِلَّا مَا سَعَىٰ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This clause is coordinated with “that none bears another’s burden” and is also among the teachings in the scrolls of Abraham and Moses.
rows.anchor: قوله: {وأن ليس للإنسان إلا ما سعى} عطف على قوله: {ألا تزر}

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqātil reads it as allowing a person in the afterlife only what that person did in worldly life.
rows.anchor: والمعنى: ليس للإنسان في الآخرة إلا ما عمل في الدنيا، قاله مقاتل

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq explains that a person receives only the recompense of their striving: good for good and evil for evil; al-Wāḥidī calls this the apparent meaning.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق: معناه: ليس له إلا جزاء سعيه، إن عمل خيرا

rows.speaker: الوالبي عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, through al-Wālibī, says the rule was abrogated for this community by 52:21: children enter Paradise through their parents’ righteousness and have their ranks raised without earning them.
rows.anchor: روى الوالبي عن ابن عباس أن هذا منسوخ الحكم في هذه الشريعة بقوله

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: ʿIkrima says the rule applied to the communities of Abraham and Moses, whereas this community may benefit from others’ deeds performed on its behalf.
rows.anchor: ونحو هذا قال عكرمة: كان ذلك لقوم إبراهيم وموسى، فأما هذه الأمة

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: A woman told the Prophet her father died without performing pilgrimage, and he told her to perform it for him, evidence for proxy worship.
rows.anchor: بدليل حديث المرأة التي قالت لرسول الله -صلى الله عليه وسلم-

rows.speaker: أصحابنا
rows.claim: The author’s legal school says the verse bars proxy performance of devotional acts except where evidence permits it, such as pilgrimage, if the rule is not abrogated.
rows.anchor: وقال العلماء من أصحابنا: هذه الآية تدل على منع النيابة في الطاعات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ruling turns on abrogation: without it, proxy worship is barred except for established exceptions; on al-Wālibī and ʿIkrima’s account, it is abrogated in Islamic law.
rows.anchor: وهذا إذا قلنا إنه غير منسوخ الحكم، وعلى ما ذكر الوالبي وعكرمة

rows.speaker: الحسين بن الفضل
rows.claim: Al-Ḥusayn b. al-Faḍl says the verse states justice, while God may graciously multiply good deeds as He wills.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسين بن الفضل (¬6): هذا من طريق العدل ليس للإنسان إلا ما سعى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yurā is passive of “I showed him”; the striving will be seen at the Resurrection, meaning the deeds will be visible in the balance, as Muqātil and al-Zajjāj say.
rows.anchor: يرى من أريته الشيء، والمعنى أن سعيه يرى يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: ابن قتيبة
rows.claim: Ibn Qutayba reads yurā as “will be known,” meaning people will know the person’s striving.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن قتيبة {يرى} يعلم، والمعنى يعلمه الناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The servants’ endpoint and return are to God; this is the exegetes’ interpretation.
rows.anchor: قوله تعالى: {وأن إلى ربك المنتهى} أي إليه منتهى العباد ومرجعهم

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: An alternative interpretation attributed to the Prophet says: “No reflection about the Lord.”
rows.anchor: وروي تفسير آخر لهذه الآية مرفوعا إلى النبي -صلى الله عليه وسلم- قال: "لا فكرة في الرب"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A person can think through created things but cannot comprehend God’s knowledge, essence, or modality; God is the endpoint of thought in this respect.
rows.anchor: فلا يحيط به علما ولا يدركه بفكرته

rows.speaker: أنس
rows.claim: A report from Anas says the Prophet taught: when God is mentioned, stop.
rows.anchor: ما روى أنس أن النبي

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: The Prophet taught people to reflect on creation and not on the Creator.
rows.anchor: وقال -صلى الله عليه وسلم-: "تفكروا في الخلق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-muntahā means the endpoint or termination.
rows.anchor: والمنتهى معناه الانتهاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God enriches people with wealth and supplies them with funds.
rows.anchor: أي أغنى الناس بالأموال ومولهم

rows.speaker: أبو صالح
rows.claim: Abū Ṣāliḥ says aqnā means giving acquired property and assets kept for future use.
rows.anchor: فقال أبو صالح: أعطى القنية وأصول الأموال التي تقتنى

rows.speaker: مجاهد ومقاتل وعكرمة عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: The majority, including Mujāhid, Muqātil, and ʿIkrima from Ibn ʿAbbās, say aqnā means making a poor person content with what was given.
rows.anchor: والاكثرون قالوا: أقنى قنع ورضى بما أعطى الفقير

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة والمبرد وابن الأعرابي
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda, al-Mubarrad, and Ibn al-Aʿrābī prefer the first sense: giving people enduring property or a reserve.
rows.anchor: والقول الأول اختيار أبي عبيدة، والمبرد، وابن الأعرابي

rows.speaker: ابن الأعرابي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Aʿrābī glosses aqnā as giving what can be stored after basic needs are met.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن الأعرابي: أقنى أعطاه ما يدخر بعد الكفاية

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq mentions both main interpretations, which al-Wāḥidī says return to one underlying root.
rows.anchor: وأبو إساق ذكر القولين (¬4)، وهما يرجعان إلى أصل واحد

rows.speaker: الليث
rows.claim: Al-Layth says qaniytu bihi means being content with it and aqnaytu property means making it a valued reserve; a line by al-Mutalammis uses aqnū for contentment.
rows.anchor: قال الليث: يقال: قنيت به، أي: رضيت

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: A second poetic usage gives aqnū the sense “I retain and preserve,” supporting a root of keeping and holding.
rows.anchor: وقال غيره: أقنو ألزم وأحفظ

rows.speaker: الضحاك والحسن وقتادة
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Ḥasan, and Qatāda say God enriches through money and gives servants as property, restricting aqnā to servants.
rows.anchor: قال الضحاك، والحسن، وقتادة: أغنى في المال وأقنى في الخدم

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says aghnā means increased and aqnā means decreased; al-Wāḥidī rejects “decreased” as linguistically unsupported unless it means contentment with little.
rows.anchor: وأما ما روي عن ابن زيد أنه قال: أغنى أكثر وأقنى أقل

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reports that polytheists asked the Messenger to split the moon in two as proof; he asked whether they would believe if he did, and they agreed. It was a Badr night.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: اجتمع المشركون إلى رسول الله

rows.speaker: عامة أهل اللغة والمفسرين
rows.claim: Most linguists and exegetes define najm as ground vegetation without a trunk, and shajar as trunked vegetation that lasts through winter, unlike najm.
rows.anchor: قال عامة أهل اللغة والمفسرين: النجم: النبت على الأرض

rows.speaker: ابن الأعرابي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Aʿrābī says najma is a small plant, plural najm; najama can mean to emerge or sprout, as a horn, star, or tooth rising.
rows.anchor: قال ابن الأعرابي: النجمة نبتة صغيرة وجمعها نجم

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة عن الحارث بن ظالم
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda cites al-Ḥārith b. Ẓālim’s line as evidence for najm meaning a plant the donkey tries to uproot.
rows.anchor: وأنشد أبو عبيدة للحارث بن ظالم (¬2): أخصيي حمار ظل يكدم نجمة

rows.speaker: الأزهري
rows.claim: Al-Azharī explains that the donkey’s effort to pull out the plant strains its body, accounting for the poem’s wording.
rows.anchor: قال الأزهري: وإنما قال ذلك لأن الحمار إذا أراد أن يقلع النجمة

rows.speaker: الليث
rows.claim: Al-Layth cites a verse describing a garment woven from abundant najm, as poetic evidence for the plant sense.
rows.anchor: وأنشد الليث: موزر بعميم النجم تنسجه

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: Exegetes take najm as what the earth has sprouted; al-Wāḥidī has not found linguists using anjama to mean “to grow.”
rows.anchor: ذكر المفسرون في تفسير النجم: هو ما أنجمت الأرض

rows.speaker: الفراء والكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ and al-Kisāʾī say Arabic often gives two nonhuman plurals one singular verb, though dual agreement is possible; dual agreement here matches the line endings.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء والكسائي: العرب إذا جمعت جمعين من غير الناس

rows.speaker: أهل التفسير
rows.claim: Exegetes explain the plants’ prostration as the prostration of their shadows.
rows.anchor: وقال أهل التفسير في معنى سجود النجم والشجر أنه سجود أظلالهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author links the prostration of shadows to 16:48.
rows.anchor: وقد ذكرنا ذلك في قوله: {يتفيأ ظلاله عن اليمين والشمائل

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid identifies najm as the stars of heaven and says the trees prostrate morning and evening.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد في قوله: {والنجم} قال نجوم السماء

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda also identifies najm here as the stars.
rows.anchor: وهو قول قتادة في النجم

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq allows the literal prostration of the stars, since God says that stars prostrate to Him.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق (¬4): وهذا جائز أن يكون الله أعلمنا أن النجم يسجد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command is not to exceed justice in the balance.
rows.anchor: أي لا تجاوزوا العدل

rows.speaker: الفراء والزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ and al-Zajjāj give two constructions: “lest you transgress,” with taṭghaw accusative, or explanatory “that you not transgress,” with it jussive as a prohibition.
rows.anchor: ذكر ذلك الفراء والزجاج (¬4)، قال الفراء: والنهي

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ prefers the prohibitive, jussive construction based on the following wording.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء: والنهي أحب إلي؛ لقوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People are not questioned to discover their sins or distinguish sinners from others; they are questioned instead for rebuke and blame.
rows.anchor: يعني: لا يسأل ليعرف ذلك بالمسألة

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqātil says they are not asked because God has already enumerated their deeds.
rows.anchor: وهذا معنى قول مقاتل: لا يسأل لأن الله قد أحصى عمله

rows.speaker: الحسن وقتادة والعوفي عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan, Qatāda, and al-ʿAwfī from Ibn ʿAbbās say angels recorded the deeds, so people are not asked what they did but why they did it.
rows.anchor: قالوا: لا يسألون ليعرف ذلك من جهتهم، لأن الملائكة قد كتبت عليهم أعمالهم

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says they are not questioned to identify criminals, since their marks identify them, as 55:41 says.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: لا يسألون ليعرف المجرمون فإنهم يعرفون بسيماهم

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: ʿIkrima says there are some stations where they are questioned and others where they are not.
rows.anchor: وقال عكرمة: إنها مواقف يسأل في بعضها ولا يسأل في بعضها

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī says the verse concerns the period after the accounting has ended.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي: هذا الفراغ من الحساب

rows.speaker: ابن قتيبة
rows.claim: Ibn Qutayba adopts the post-accounting view: people are questioned during the long Judgment Day, then speech and dispute cease and groups are known by their faces.
rows.anchor: واختار ابن قتيبة هذا القول وشرحه فقال: إن يوم القيامة كما قال الله

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj’s view is that people are not asked an information-seeking question about their sins.
rows.anchor: أحدها: لا يسألون سؤال استفهام عن ذنوبهم، وهو اختيار الزجاج

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ’s view is that people are not questioned in order to identify them by their sins.
rows.anchor: والثاني: لا يسألون ليعفروا بذنوبهم وهو اختيار الفراء

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqātil glosses the pair as a human and a jinni.
rows.anchor: قال مقاتل: يقول إنسي ولا جني

rows.speaker: ثعلب عن عمرو عن أبيه
rows.claim: Thaʿlab, citing ʿAmr from his father, says al-jānn is one of the jinn and its plural is jinān.
rows.anchor: قال ثعلب، عن عمرو، عن أبيه: الجان من الجن وجمعه جنان

rows.speaker: جماعة المفسرين
rows.claim: A group of exegetes says criminals are recognized by black faces and blue eyes, citing 3:106 and 20:102.
rows.anchor: قال جماعة المفسرين: يعرف بسواد الوجوه وزرقة الأعين

rows.speaker: عطاء عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: ʿAṭāʾ from Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the criminals as Abū Jahl, al-Aswad, al-Walīd, and al-Naḍr.
rows.anchor: قال عطاء عن ابن عباس في تفسير المجرمين في هذه الآية: يريد أبا جهل

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī says angels seize them by the forelocks while they are on the bridge and hurl them into the Fire.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي: تأخذهم الملائكة وهم على الصراط بنواصيهم

rows.speaker: الأعمش عن رجل عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-Aʿmash reports from an unnamed man from Ibn ʿAbbās that they are seized by forelock and feet, broken like firewood, and thrown into an oven.
rows.anchor: وروى الأعمش عن رجل عن ابن عباس قال يؤخذ بناصيته وقدميه فيكسر

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq says their feet are bound behind them to their forelocks before they are thrown into the Fire, intensifying punishment and humiliation.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو إسحاق نجعل الأقدام مضمومة إلى النواصي من خلف

none: source text is broken after an incomplete citation

rows.speaker: الفراء والزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ and al-Zajjāj allow two parses: the first al-sābiqūn is subject and the second predicate (those foremost in obedience are foremost to mercy), or the second is emphasis and the next clause is the predicate.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء والزجاج يجوز أن يكون (والسابقون) ابتداء، وخبره الثاني

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās identifies them as those who preceded others in affirming God’s oneness and believing His Messenger, as in 9:100.
rows.anchor: فقال ابن عباس (¬1): يريد الذين سبقوا إلى توحيد الله

rows.speaker: ابن سيرين
rows.claim: Ibn Sīrīn identifies them as those who prayed toward both qiblas, an early group of the Companions and thus close to Ibn ʿAbbās’s view.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن سيرين: هم الذين صلوا القبلتين

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: ʿIkrima says they were the first to accept Islam.
rows.anchor: ونحو هذا قال عكرمة: السابقون إلى الإسلام

rows.speaker: الربيع
rows.claim: Al-Rabīʿ describes them as the first to answer the Messenger.
rows.anchor: وهو معنى قول الربيع: إلى إجابة الرسول

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqātil says they were first to believe in the prophets, restricting them to the earliest of this community.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل: إلى الأنبياء بالإيمان

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī says the first to follow the Messenger in each community will be first to Paradise in the afterlife.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي: السابقون إلى الرسول من كل أمة

rows.speaker: أكثر المفسرين
rows.claim: Most exegetes understand precedence as precedence in obedience; al-Quraẓī broadly includes every good and all God’s invitations, the choice of Ibn Kaysān.
rows.anchor: وأكثر المفسرين جعلوا هذا السبق إلى الطاعات، فمنهم من أجملها

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿīd b. Jubayr specifies repentance as the act in which they were foremost.
rows.anchor: فقال سعيد بن جبير: إلى التوبة

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: ʿAlī specifies the five daily prayers.
rows.anchor: وقال علي -رضي الله عنه-: إلى الصلوات الخمس

rows.speaker: عثمان بن أبي سودة
rows.claim: ʿUthmān b. Abī Sawda specifies going early to the mosque and jihad, in the first ranks of worshippers and fighters.
rows.anchor: وقال عثمان بن أبي سودة (¬2): إلى المسجد، إلى الجهاد

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās compares the brought-near to the prophets and messengers.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: مثل النبيين والمرسلين

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī says their destination is Eden.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي: إلى عدن

rows.speaker: أهل المعاني
rows.claim: The specialists in meaning describe their reward as God’s abundant recompense and great honor.
rows.anchor: وقال أهل المعاني: جزيل ثواب الله وعظيم كرامته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God has no need of their faith or worship.
rows.anchor: أي عن إيمانهم وعبادتهم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās explains protecting yourselves as avoiding what God forbids and doing what He commands.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: أي بالانتهاء عما نهاكم الله عنه، والعمل بطاعته

rows.speaker: عمر عن النبي
rows.claim: ʿUmar asks how to protect one’s family; the Prophet answers: forbid them what God forbids and command them what He commands.
rows.anchor: قال عمر: يا رسول الله: هذا نقي أنفسنا فكيف لنا بأهلينا؟ قال: "تنهونهم

rows.speaker: مقاتل بن حيان
rows.claim: Muqātil b. Ḥayyān says a Muslim must discipline himself and his family, teach good, and forbid evil, including for dependants and enslaved people.
rows.anchor: قال مقاتل بن حيان: يعني أن يؤدب الرجل المسلم نفسه وأهله

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: ʿAlī says the verse commands people to teach and discipline their families.
rows.anchor: في هذه الآية: علموهم وأدبوهم

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan says to command the family to obey God and forbid them to disobey Him.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: تأمرهم بطاعة الله وتنهاهم عن معصيته

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda likewise says to command obedience to God and forbid disobedience.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: مروهم بطاعة الله، وانهوهم عن معصية الله

rows.speaker: ابن عمر
rows.claim: Ibn ʿUmar tells a man to discipline his child, since the father is accountable for how he raised and taught the child, while the child is accountable for honoring and obeying him.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عمر لرجل: أدب ابنك فإنك مسؤول عن ولدك

rows.speaker: أبو ذر عن النبي
rows.claim: Abū Dharr reports the Prophet advising: be gentle with your family and do not withhold their provision.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو ذر: أوصاني رسول الله -صلى الله عليه وسلم-

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq says to direct oneself and one’s family toward what brings one near God and keep them from sins.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو إسحاق: المعنى: خذوا أنفسكم وأهليكم

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqātil says good discipline protects the family from sins and the Fire; the author refers to his earlier explanation of the Fire’s fuel in 2:24.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل: قوا أنفسكم وأهليكم المعاصي بالأدب الصالح

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the angels over Hell as its nineteen keepers.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يريد خزنة النار تسعة عشر ملكا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The angels are severe toward Hell’s inhabitants, as in 9:73 and 66:9; alternatively, “severe” can describe their large bodies.
rows.anchor: أي على أهل النار كقوله: {واغلظ عليهم}

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومقاتل
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the distance between an angel’s shoulders is a year’s journey; Muqātil gives a similar description.
rows.anchor: قال (¬2) ابن عباس: ما بين منكبيه مسيرة سنة

rows.speaker: مجاهد ومقاتل والسدي
rows.claim: Mujāhid, Muqātil, and al-Suddī identify nūn as the whale carrying the earth in a sea beneath the lowest earth.
rows.anchor: وقول مجاهد ومقاتل والسدي (¬2)، قالوا: هو الحوت الذي يحمل الأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Arabic, nūn means fish; the Qurʾān uses it in Jonah’s epithet Dhū al-Nūn.
rows.anchor: والنون في اللغة السمكة (¬4). ومنه قوله تعالى في ذكر يونس

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: Saʿīd b. Jubayr reports from Ibn ʿAbbās that nūn means an inkpot; al-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Ḥasan, and Qatāda also hold this view.
rows.anchor: وروى سعيد بن جبير عن ابن عباس قال: (ن) الدواة

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: A poetic line uses nūn to mean inkpot.
rows.anchor: ومنه قول الشاعر (¬4): إذا ما الشوق برح بي إليهم

rows.speaker: عكرمة عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: ʿIkrima reports from Ibn ʿAbbās that nūn is the final letter of al-Raḥmān; alif-lām-rā, ḥā-mīm, and nūn are disjointed letters of that name.
rows.anchor: وروى عكرمة (¬5) عن ابن عباس أن نون هاهنا آخر حروف الرحمن

rows.speaker: معاوية بن قرة
rows.claim: A report raised to the Prophet says nūn here is a tablet of light.
rows.anchor: وروى معاوية بن قرة (¬7) مرفوعا أن نون هاهنا لوح من نور

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة وابن كيسان
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda and Ibn Kaysān say nūn is a surah-opening letter like the other disjointed openings.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيدة وابن كيسان (¬1): نون فاتحة السورة كسائر الفواتح

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad says nūn is the name of an alphabet letter like qāf and mīm; this is likelier because a fish-name would decline, whereas alphabet names are paused.
rows.anchor: وقال المبرد: (ن) اسم الحرف المعروف من حروف الهجاء نحو (ق) و (م). وهذا هو الأشبه

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad favors interpreting nūn as an alphabet opener, specifically the final letter of al-Raḥmān, since it is built on a vowelless pause.
rows.anchor: وقال المبرد: (ن) اسم الحرف المعروف من حروف الهجاء

rows.speaker: القراء
rows.claim: Readers differ on pronouncing nūn clearly or assimilating it before “by the pen”; clear pronunciation treats it as paused, while concealment treats it as connected.
rows.anchor: والقراء مختلفون في إظهار النون وإخفائه من قوله {ن * والقلم}

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ prefers clear pronunciation because the letter is spelled out, and spelled letters are like pauses even when connected.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء: وإظهارها أعجب إلي، لأنها هجاء، والهجاء كالوقوف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author refers to his discussion of the same pronunciation issue at 38:1 and 36:1–2.
rows.anchor: وقد ذكرنا هذا في قوله: {ص * والقرآن}

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the first thing God created was the pen, which He commanded to write everything that would happen until the Hour; it is a pen of light as long as the distance between heaven and earth.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: أول ما خلق الله القلم ثم قال له: اكتب ما هو كائن

rows.speaker: مجاهد عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: Mujāhid reports from Ibn ʿAbbās that God first created the pen and commanded it to write destiny through the Resurrection; people follow a decree already completed.
rows.anchor: وروى مجاهد عنه قال: كان أول (¬2) ما خلق الله القلم فقال له: اكتب القدر

rows.speaker: جميع المفسرين
rows.claim: All exegetes identify the pen as the one that wrote the Preserved Tablet.
rows.anchor: وهذا قول جميع المفسرين. قالوا: هو القلم الذي كتب به اللوح المحفوظ

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: Exegetes say “what they write” refers to the recording angels’ records of human deeds.
rows.anchor: قالوا: يعني وما تكتب الملائكة

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq parses anta as the noun of mā, bimajnūn as its predicate, and bi-naʿmati rabbika as attached to the negation: by your Lord’s favor, madness is denied of you.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق: {أنت} هو اسم {ما}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse answers the accusation in 15:6 that the recipient of the Reminder is mad.
rows.anchor: وهذا جواب لقوله: {يا أيها الذي نزل عليه الذكر إنك لمجنون}

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqātil says the Meccan unbelievers called Muḥammad mad, so God swore by the whale, pen, and human deeds; “by your Lord’s favor” means by His mercy.
rows.anchor: قال مقاتل: وذلك حين قال كفار مكة: إن محمدا مجنون

rows.speaker: عطاء عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: ʿAṭāʾ from Ibn ʿAbbās says the blessing is God’s gift of faith and prophethood.
rows.anchor: وقال عطاء عن (¬5) ابن عباس: يريد بنعمة ربك عليك بالإيمان والنبوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author introduces the verse as praise of the Prophet accompanied by a promise of reward.
rows.anchor: ثم مدحه مع وعد الأجر بقوله: {وإنك لعلى خلق عظيم}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The deniers are Meccan leaders who invited the Prophet to adopt their religion; God forbids him to obey them.
rows.anchor: يعني رؤساء أهل مكة، وذلك أنهم دعوه إلى دين

rows.speaker: الليث
rows.claim: Al-Layth glosses idhān as softness and accommodation.
rows.anchor: قال الليث: الإدهان: اللين والمصانعة

rows.speaker: أبو الهيثم
rows.claim: Abū al-Haytham defines idhān as verbal accommodation and softening one’s speech.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو الهيثم: الإدهان: المقاربة في الكلام والتليين في القول

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad says the related verbs describe betrayal in religion or acting outwardly against what one inwardly holds.
rows.anchor: وقال المبرد: أدهن الرجل في دينه، وداهن في أمره، إذا خان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author refers to his discussion of “you are compromising” at 56:81.
rows.anchor: وذكرنا هذا عند قوله: {أنتم مدهنون}

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī says they wanted the Prophet to compromise in religion so they would compromise in turn, each leaving what the other disliked.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي: لو (¬1) تصانعهم في الدين

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says they wanted the Prophet to incline toward them and abandon the truth, so they would side with him; this is the majority view and the meaning of al-Wālibī’s report from Ibn ʿAbbās.
rows.anchor: وهذا قول مجاهد: تركن إليهم وتترك ما أنت عليه من الحق

rows.speaker: ابن قتيبة
rows.claim: Ibn Qutayba says they wanted the Prophet to worship their idols for a time and for them to worship God for a time.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن قتيبة: كانوا أرادوه على أن يعبدوا آلهتهم مدة

rows.speaker: عطاء عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: ʿAṭāʾ from Ibn ʿAbbās says they wanted him to disbelieve so they would disbelieve; Muqātil, ʿAṭiyya, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk give the same view, which the author treats as a form of the first compromise interpretation.
rows.anchor: وروى عنه عطاء: لو تكفر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The day phrase attaches to the preceding challenge: if their claimed partners are real, let them bring them on Judgment Day to benefit and intercede, but those claims fail.
rows.anchor: يقول الله: {إن كانوا صادقين} في أنها شركاء فليأتوا بها يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: عكرمة عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: ʿIkrima reports from Ibn ʿAbbās that “uncovering the shin” means severe distress, citing an Arabic line about war rising on a leg.
rows.anchor: روى عكرمة عن ابن عباس قال: عن شدة. ألم تسمع إلى قول الشاعر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says unclear Qurʾānic language should be sought in poetry, the Arabs’ record; he calls the verse a day of distress and hardship.
rows.anchor: وسئل ابن عباس عن هذه الآية فقال: إذا خفي عليكم شيء من القرآن

rows.speaker: عطاء عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: ʿAṭāʾ from Ibn ʿAbbās explains it as hardship in the afterlife.
rows.anchor: وروى عطاء عنه قال: يريد شدة في الآخرة

rows.speaker: إبراهيم عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibrāhīm from Ibn ʿAbbās explains it as the severity of the event.
rows.anchor: وروى إبراهيم عنه أيضا: عن شدة الأمر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Another report from Ibn ʿAbbās calls it the disclosure of a tremendous matter.
rows.anchor: قال (¬4): وقال ابن عباس يكشف عن أمر عظيم

rows.speaker: مجاهد عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: Mujāhid reports from Ibn ʿAbbās that it is the most severe hour of the Resurrection; Saʿīd b. Jubayr, Mujāhid, and Qatāda likewise call it severe distress and great affliction.
rows.anchor: وروى مجاهد عنه قال: هو أشد ساعة في القيامة

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda says Arabs use “the matter uncovered its shin” for an intensifying crisis or war, citing Qays b. Zuhayr.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عبيدة: إذا اشتد الأمر والحرب قيل: قد كشف الأمر عن ساقه

rows.speaker: الفراء عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ transmits from Ibn ʿAbbās that it is the Resurrection and Hour because of their severity, and cites an Arab poem.
rows.anchor: وروى الفراء بإسناده (¬5) عن ابن عباس (¬6) أنه قال: يريد يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq interprets it as the revelation of a severe crisis and cites a poem about war’s shin being bared.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو إسحاق: معنى {يكشف عن ساق} كشف عن الأمر الشديد

rows.speaker: ابن قتيبة
rows.claim: Ibn Qutayba derives the idiom from a person in a great task pulling up his garment to work; exposing the shin became a metaphor for distress, supported by Arabic verse.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن قتيبة: أصل هذا أن الرجل إذا وقع (¬4) في أمر عظيم يحتاج إلى معاناته

rows.speaker: غيره
rows.claim: Another explanation paraphrases the verse as the day matters become as severe as a task requiring the shin to be uncovered; the expression became a proverb for hardship.
rows.anchor: وزاد غيره بيانا فقال: تأويل الآية: يوم يشتد الأمر

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqātil says unbelievers’ spines will be fused into one bone like cattle horns because they did not prostrate to God in worldly life.
rows.anchor: قال مقاتل: وذلك أنه تدمج أصلاب الكفار يومئذ فيكون عظما واحدا

rows.speaker: جميع المفسرين
rows.claim: All exegetes say creatures prostrate once, but unbelievers and hypocrites then cannot prostrate because their backs have stiffened.
rows.anchor: وهذا قول جميع المفسرين (¬2). قالوا: إذا كان ذلك

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd says believers fall prostrate, while hypocrites’ backs become board-like, as if containing spits or skewers.
rows.anchor: قال ابن مسعود: وأما المؤمنون فيخرون سجدا
